doc: The six list rules the Place (stop-detail) screen is assembled from. A place is N member poles at one kerb (ADR-042) — a lone stop is a place with one — and each pole carries its own routes, its own live readings and its own walk. `boardingPoleId` decides which member pole a route row belongs to, which matters only where upstream published one physical pole under two stop ids and the build folded them onto one member (WP5-11) — the wire keeps both ids so that nothing a rider saved stops resolving, and this is the map back. `dedupeRoutes` decides which route rows a rider sees, by collapsing the operators' service-type variants to one row per rider line (operator + number + direction, at one pole) and keeping the one carrying a reading. `dedupeRoutes` takes the member list too, so the same three rows state what the fold does and does not change: two ids of one pole collapse to one row, and the surviving row keeps the id upstream gave it — because that id is the key a favourite is saved under. `operatorsOf` names the operators for the 'served by' line, in first-seen order. `orderPoles` decides what order the pole groups (and their map dots) appear in, in three tiers: the pole the rider arrived from, then nearest, then the dataset's own member order. `poleSideOctants` decides whether a pole's heading needs a compass side to tell it apart from a sibling's, and which side that is. Every row below is built from a real dataset build — real canonical ids, real names in all three locales, real service-type variants — because the shapes that break these rules (a number run by two operators, a loop whose two directions share a destination, one minibus number covering two different services, one stop code printed on two poles a metre apart) are ones nobody invents; the first three groups are from the build of 2026-07-27, `poleSideOctants` and `boardingPoleId` from `d598893de6add2e4` of 2026-07-31, and `dedupeRoutes`' three folded-pole rows from `1ccad7436a8df480` — the first build the fold shipped in. Live readings are the one synthetic part: they are stated against a fixed `nowIso` of 2026-07-27T12:00:00+08:00, since a fixture that read a clock would be worthless to a second platform. ONE ROW IS `knownDefect` — read it before changing the dedupe key.

boardingPoleId.doc: Which boarding point a pole id belongs to, given the place's members. `args.poleId` is the id a route row departs from (or the one a `?pole=` deep link names), `args.members` is the place's member list exactly as `/v1/stop/:id` sends it, and `expect` is the pole id to group that row under. A member answers with itself; an id listed in some member's `aliasIds` answers with that member; anything else comes back unchanged, so an id from an older build degrades to 'not one of these poles' rather than to nothing. Every row is Tin Shui Wai Park or its neighbour Tin Shui Estate, because between them they hold both answers: the park's `KMB:DC5B5F4350685442` and `KMB:AFB9321F7CD2C2E4` are 1.11 m apart — one grid step of latitude — with the same operator, the same name in all three locales and the same printed code TN510, so the build folds the second onto the first; the estate's two TN507 poles are 22.88 m apart and identical in every other field, and are deliberately NOT folded. Distance is not the rule on its own: TN511 shares a coordinate exactly with the surviving TN510 pole and is not folded either, because its printed code differs and a rider can read it.

cases.why: The first render, before the query resolves: the screen calls this with an empty member list. It answers with the id it was given rather than throwing, because a place that has not loaded yet is not a place saying this pole is somewhere else.

dedupeRoutes.doc: One row per rider line, in first-appearance order, keeping the entry that carries a live reading. The key is `operator|routeNo|bound` plus the pole the row boards at — deliberately not the service type (riders do not choose one); see the two knownDefect rows for what the pole costs. That pole is the row's **boarding point** when `args.members` is given and its raw `stopId` when it is not: where upstream published one physical pole under two ids the build folds them onto one member (WP5-11), and passing the member list is what collapses the two into one row. Replacing a keyed entry keeps the position its first variant held, so the list does not reshuffle when a reading arrives on a later variant. `expect` states the surviving entries as route id + the pole they depart from, because both halves matter: the pole files the row under a heading, and — since it is also the key `SaveStar` persists — the surviving row must come back with the id upstream gave it and never with the one it is displayed under.

cases.name: three-citybus-service-types-at-one-pole-are-one-row
cases.why: The everyday case, taken verbatim from the shipped dataset: Citybus lists 969 three times at Tin Shui Wai Park, all outbound, all bound for Causeway Bay, all from the same kerb. A rider choosing between three identical-looking rows is the failure this rule exists to prevent. The survivor is the first, and its serviceType is not part of the key.

cases.name: a-variant-with-a-live-reading-replaces-one-without
cases.why: Service type 2 is the only 969 with a reading, so it takes the row even though type 1 came first — and type 3, which has none, does not then take it back. A port that wrote `if (!existing) set` would show a blank row while a bus was four minutes away; one that wrote `set` unconditionally would lose the reading to the variant behind it.

cases.name: the-first-live-variant-wins-even-when-a-later-one-is-sooner
cases.why: WRONG, PINNED SO EVERY PLATFORM IS WRONG IDENTICALLY. KMB runs 269D from Tin Shui Wai Park as service types 1 and 4 off the same pole. Here type 1 is 18 minutes away and type 4 is 3 minutes away — same number, same direction, same destination (LEK YUEN), so to a rider they are one bus — and the rule keeps type 1 because it appeared first. The screen therefore says 18 min while the next 269D is 3 min away. The edge's `dedupeEtas` collapses on the identical key and keeps the SOONER arrival, so Nearby and Place detail can disagree about the same route at the same kerb, which is how this surfaces. Once fixed, `expect` becomes the `KMB:269D:outbound:4` entry and the tie-break reads: prefer a live reading, then the sooner first arrival, then first appearance.

cases.name: the-same-number-from-two-operators-stays-two-rows
cases.why: Route 104 is jointly run: Citybus and KMB both list it inbound at Sands Street, and the same-kerb merge puts both poles on one screen. Only the operator in the key keeps them apart — drop it and one of the two feeds silently stops being shown, at exactly the places where a rider has a genuine choice of which bus to flag down.

cases.name: both-directions-of-one-number-stay-two-rows
cases.why: Citybus 26 passes Statue Square in both directions and — because it is a loop — BOTH directions are labelled 'Lai Tak Tsuen'. So the destination cannot separate them and the bound must. Key on the number alone and half the riders board a bus going the wrong way round.

cases.name: a-line-boarding-two-poles-keeps-a-row-at-each
cases.why: THE ROW THAT PINNED THE DEFECT, NOW PINNING THE FIX — and it exercises both halves of the key at once. Three 269D entries at Tin Shui Wai Park across two poles: service types 1 and 4 board at KMB:AFB9321F7CD2C2E4, type 3 at KMB:DC5B5F4350685442, and only type 3 has a reading. Before Wave 5 the key omitted the pole, so all three fused and 'keep the one with a reading' also decided which pole group the row was filed under — the row LEFT AFB9…'s group and joined DC5B…'s, and would move back when the reading did. Now: same-pole variants still collapse (types 1 and 4 become one row, first appearance wins, which is what this function is for), and the two poles keep a row each, so nothing moves when a bus departs. This is also the place that pays the display cost: both members print the stop code TN510, so 269D now shows twice under two identically-labelled pole headings until a heading is labelled by something that distinguishes it. A port that dropped `stopId` from the key files a row under the wrong kerb; a port that dropped it from the OUTPUT cannot file it at all.

cases.name: one-minibus-number-at-two-poles-loses-a-destination
cases.why: Two different green-minibus services both numbered 20 leave Tai On Street: `GMB:20:outbound:2002320` from pole GMB:20000270 for Chai Wan (Fung Yip Street), and `GMB:20:outbound:2002319` from pole GMB:20009406 for Chai Wan Industrial City. They share operator, number and direction, and both are circular so both are 'outbound' on every leg — direction cannot separate them either. FIXED in Wave 5 by putting the member pole in the key: one row per line PER POLE. Before the fix the two fused, the second destination was never shown, and where route 20 was a pole's only route the pole's whole group vanished from the list while its dot stayed on the map (21 poles emptied in the 2026-07-27 build; 44 rider lines span more than one pole and 26 of those have differing destinations, GMB most of all). The live merge then made it worse: /v1/etas/:id collapses readings across the whole place, so only one pole's row could be filled and the survivor — chosen by which row had a reading — moved between kerbs as buses departed (measured 2026-07-31: GMB 68K, both poles publishing 11 s apart). The old comment claimed the fusion was safe because 'route_code is unique within a region': true of the code, not of the number on the front of the bus. Residual, deliberately not fixed here: the edge still dedupes across poles, so at most one of a line's poles carries a reading and the other reads 'no reading right now' even when a bus is due there — that needs the canonical model to carry a reading per boarding point, which is a wire change with its own owner. A port that keyed on operator|routeNo|bound alone passes every other row here and fails this one.

operatorsOf.doc: The distinct operators serving a place, each once, in the order the route list first mentions them. First-seen, not sorted: the caller passes the deduped route list, so the operator that leads the label is the one that leads the list under it. A merged `P:` id has no operator of its own, which is why this is derived from the routes rather than parsed from the id.

cases.name: an-operator-seen-again-later-is-listed-once

orderPoles.doc: The member poles in display order, by three tiers: (1) the pole named by the incoming `?pole=`, if it is a member; (2) nearest first, but only where a distance is known for both poles; (3) the order the server sent, which is stable across renders and across a location fix arriving. `expect` is the pole ids in order. `distanceM` is an object keyed by pole id — a partial object means only those poles have been measured, and an empty one means the rider is unlocated.

poleSideOctants.doc: Which compass side each pole of a place sits on — returned ONLY for poles whose heading would otherwise be indistinguishable from another pole's, and only where the geometry can honestly answer. `args.poles` is each member's canonical id, its own coordinate and the heading text a renderer already prints for it; `expect` maps id → octant (0–7 clockwise from North, the same scale as `geo#bearingOctant`) and OMITS every pole that gets nothing, which is the overwhelming majority. The octant is the bearing from the centroid of the *colliding* poles, not of the whole place. Every row is real: the members, their coordinates and their names are verbatim from the dataset build of 2026-07-31 (`d598893de6add2e4`), where 567 of 10 118 places print a duplicate pole heading, 226 of them can be told apart this way and 9 892 places are untouched. The kernel returns a number and never a word — `core` owns the rule, `i18n` owns the word (ADR-054).

cases.name: a-lone-stop-gets-nothing
cases.why: A place with one member. There is nothing to tell apart, so the heading must come through untouched — this is 7 721 of the 10 118 places in the shipped build and the rule's restraint starts here.

cases.name: an-ordinary-multi-pole-place-with-distinct-headings-gets-nothing
cases.why: Cheerful Park, Pak Wo Road, verbatim from the shipped build — and it carries BOTH answers at once, which is why it is one row rather than two. The lone Citybus pole and KMB's ND127 already print unique headings and get nothing; ND126 is printed on two poles 35.4 m apart, so those two, and only those two, are given a side. A port that returned a side for every member of a place with any collision would pass a single-collision row and fail this one.

cases.name: two-poles-with-no-stop-code-at-all-become-north-and-south
cases.why: The commonest shape by a wide margin, and the one the plan's row did not name: 507 of the 571 colliding groups in the shipped build are poles with NO printed stop code, so the heading is the bare operator name. Peaksville, Robinson Road has two Citybus poles 20.3 m apart, both printing just "Citybus". They come out North (0) and South (4) — opposite, because for a pair the two bearings from their midpoint are reciprocal.

cases.name: tin-shui-wai-park-two-tn510-poles-are-one-metre-apart-and-get-nothing
cases.why: The place the whole work package was raised for, all four members verbatim from the shipped build. KMB prints the stop code TN510 on two of them and their full names are identical too, so neither the code nor the name can separate them. Measured: they are 1.11 m apart — ONE coordinate grid step at the five decimal places upstream publishes — so no compass word can send a rider to one rather than the other, and any word derived from that offset flips the day a coordinate is nudged. The honest answer is nothing, and it stays nothing: this pair is one physical pole published under two upstream ids, and the remedy is in `buildPlaces`, not in a heading. A port tempted to add an ordinal here should read `poleSideOctants`' last section first.

cases.name: exactly-coincident-poles-get-nothing
cases.why: West Kowloon Cultural District, M+ — two KMB poles on stop code YT266 at byte-identical coordinates. 49 of the 64 code collisions in the shipped build are at exactly 0.0 m like this. Both bearings from the centroid are 0° (`atan2(0, 0)`), so the separation guard is what declines it; without that guard the two headings would both read "North" and the rider would be no better off while believing they had been told something.

cases.name: three-colliding-poles-where-two-share-a-side-are-all-declined
cases.why: Shau Kei Wan East Government Secondary School: three KMB poles all printing bare "KMB" in English. Two are at identical coordinates and the third is 26.3 m south, so every member clears the separation floor from the group centroid and the sides come out North / North / South. The reciprocity that saves a pair does not generalise, so distinctness is checked on its own — 14 groups in the shipped build fail exactly here. Declining the WHOLE group is deliberate: labelling them would leave two headings identical AND longer.

cases.name: the-same-place-in-chinese-has-only-two-colliding-headings
cases.why: The identical three poles, with the headings a Chinese reader sees: upstream gives KMB:E060D03C30317F2C the code ED522 in `zh-Hant`/`zh-Hans` but not in `en`. So that pole's heading is unique here, the collision is between the other two — 26.3 m apart — and they are labelled North and South while the English rendering of the same place is declined. This is why the rule takes the heading TEXT and not the pole's name or id: whether two headings collide is a property of what is printed, and what is printed depends on the locale.

poleDistinctions.doc: What each pole of a place is told apart by, in the order the data can support it (WP5-12) — the answer for the band BETWEEN the two refusals ADR-071 requires to stay different: `foldDuplicatePoles` will not merge two poles more than 2 m apart, and `poleSideOctants` will not name a compass side under 10 m, so 141 pairs across 115 places print an identical heading today. Neither threshold moves. `args.poles` is each member's canonical id, its own coordinate, the heading text a renderer already prints (which is why the flag code is already in it — `poleFlagCode` runs first) and the pole's OWN printed name. `expect` is the map as entries, and a pole with nothing to say is ABSENT from it rather than present with every field unset. The tiers: a compass side, byte-identical to `poleSideOctants`; else the pole's own name where the folded keys are pairwise distinct (`poleNameKey`, never bytes); else the group is partitioned into units by complete linkage at the same 10 m and the compass question is asked about the UNITS, with every pole of a multi-pole unit additionally `crowded`; else nothing. The invariant every row here must satisfy: two poles under one heading share an `octant` only if both are `crowded`, and every pole in a multi-pole unit is `crowded`. Every row is verbatim from build `ceb33eed99461e04`.

cases.name: a-lone-pole-is-told-nothing
cases.why: THE CONTROL for the whole rule. A lone stop is a place with one member (ADR-042) and there is nothing to distinguish it from — an implementation that answered here would put a cue on every stop in Hong Kong.

cases.name: city-hall-two-poles-get-a-compass-side-exactly-as-today
cases.why: THE ZERO-DIFF PROOF, and the reason the side tier comes first. City Hall, Connaught Road Central: the Citybus pole and the KMB pole whose Chinese name carries CW114 already print unique headings and get nothing; the other two are 18.35 m apart and get exactly the octants `poleSideOctants` gives them. 226 groups in this build reach this tier, and a port that reordered the tiers would change what all 226 print — a two-word compass cue replaced by a ~35-character name.

cases.name: queen-mary-hospital-the-poles-own-names-differ-so-the-name-is-the-answer
cases.why: The biggest win, and the shape the row that filed WP5-12 did not list: 143 declined groups have member names that DIFFER. Both minibus poles here print bare "GMB" / "專線小巴" 7.35 m apart, and the wire has carried `Queen Mary Hospital, Pok Fu Lam Road` and `POK FU LAM ROAD, near Queen Mary Hospital Wing H` all along. The Citybus pole is alone under its heading and stays silent.

cases.name: a-case-only-name-difference-is-not-a-difference
cases.why: THE ROW THAT STOPS A PORT USING `!=`. Bonham Road: the two names differ by exactly one comma, so a byte comparison would take the name tier, print the same words twice, and claim the ambiguity resolved — which is precisely what `poleSideOctants` refuses to do with a compass word it cannot support. 21 groups in this build are this shape. Folded through `poleNameKey` they are equal, so the rule falls through and says plainly that there is nothing to choose between.

cases.name: rumsey-street-two-poles-4-7-m-apart-say-so-plainly
cases.why: The acceptance's second branch, and the case WP5-12 is named for: two KMB poles 4.68 m apart with the same name and no code — too far apart to be one pole, too close for a compass word. `crowded` and no octant, because the group is ONE unit and there is no second unit to take a bearing from. The Citybus pole prints a different heading and is untouched.

cases.name: lok-hin-terrace-a-crowded-unit-and-a-far-pole-each-get-a-side
cases.why: THE MIXED PLACE, and the row that fails a port which kept `poleSideOctants`' distinctness invariant. Three poles print bare "KMB": two at the SAME coordinate and one 47–54 m away. Today all three get nothing, because the distinctness guard trips on the coincident pair. Now the pair is one unit and the far pole another, so both units get a side — the pair shares octant 5 and is `crowded`, the far pole gets octant 1 and is NOT, because calling a pole 50 m from its siblings "adjacent" would be a plain falsehood. Note the fourth KMB pole: its Chinese name carries ED516, so `poleFlagCode` lifted it out of the collision before this rule ran.

cases.name: statue-square-the-units-octants-collide-so-only-the-crowded-pair-speaks
cases.why: The last tier, and the honest floor: four KMB poles print bare "Statue Square" across 41 m, and once partitioned the units' bearings are not pairwise distinct, so no unit gets a side. The 3.49 m pair still says it is adjacent; the two poles alone in their units are told nothing, which is the 54 poles this rule leaves silent territory-wide. A row is needed for this branch precisely because it is unreachable from a two-pole fixture.

placeDetailView.doc: The whole Place screen, composed once (WP6-3). The four rules above decide *what* a rider sees; this decides what they collapse to on screen — the pole heading and its separator, the per-kerb walk, the summary line and its two separator widths, the grouping under boarding points, which poles appear at all, and the three-way readout. It lived in `apps/mobile/app/stop/[id].tsx` until now, reachable only by rendering a React tree. Words the composition needs are INJECTED (`labels`), never imported: core owns the rule, the catalogue owns the word (ADR-054).

cases.name: a-lone-stop-is-one-flat-list
cases.why: The common case: one boarding point, so `grouped` is false, `groups` is empty and every row is in `rows`. A renderer that read `groups` alone would draw an empty screen for most of Hong Kong.
